description:
GPS <Green Patrol Squad> is from Doan Thi Diem School,HN. Led by Gia Linh, with app-building experience from TITAN (Top 25 Secondary School, Samsung Solve for Tomorrow 2026), we combine product, coding and NASA research. Minh Khang leads Data Science and data-to-sound logic; collaborate by Tue Minh, Tuan Kiet & Ngoc Ha. 
Inspired by Tuệ Minh’s Green Corner and TEDx story, we turn complex NASA air-quality visuals into sound, games and questions (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1eG5ywBjDiE&t=207s)
summary:
Green Corner is a bilingual (English/Vietnamese) web app that lets middle-school students hear NASA air-quality data. We took the NASA SVS 5533 animation of the GEOS-CF model (summer 2024) and turned it into an "Earth Jukebox". At 30 cities around the world, the app reads the map colour for four pollutants and plays it as music: CO is a bowed cello, PM2.5 a kalimba, NOx an electric pluck and ozone a glass bell. A darker colour gives a higher, louder note. Students choose a city and listen to 300 moments of summer 2024 next to the moving NASA map. They read simple notes from our mascot Sprout, then test their ears in four mini-games.
This answers the challenge by translating sight into sound in real time, with accessibility at its core. It matters because NASA maps rely on colour and scientific terms, which leaves out many young learners and people who cannot rely on colour. Green Corner gives everyone another way to notice and question how our air changes.
details:
What it does and how it works

  1. Frames: from the 1,800-frame NASA video "AirQuality_MapWithLabels" (5760×3240) we sample 300 frames, 4 per day, from 1 July to mid-September 2024. The map shows four pollutant bands on a fixed latitude-longitude grid, so each city is found from its coordinates. Dates are estimated from frame order because the frames carry no time stamp.
  2. Colour to level: the map has no colour scale, so we use relative levels. For each pollutant, the median and 85th percentile of the whole map split Low, Medium and High.
  3. Level to sound: the browser synthesizes each note live. A higher level gives a higher pitch and louder volume on a pentatonic scale. Each pollutant keeps its own instrument.
  4. Three zones:
  • Sprout's Story: why we started, the NASA source, and what sonification is.
  • Summer Jukebox: one city across the summer, a "4 gases" tab to hear each instrument alone, and a whole-summer analysis (% of time at High, rank among 30 cities, Sprout's notes).
  • Four games: Air Detective, Sky Scales, Particle Dash and Green Solutions. Stars from the games decorate "My tree".

Benefits

  • A second way into the NASA map: listen first, then look and check.
  • English and Vietnamese, read-aloud, phone-sized layout, no login, no ads.
  • One HTML file that runs in a modern browser.

Intended impact

We want students aged 11–13 to practise observing, comparing, predicting and verifying Earth data, and to care about the air they breathe. Next, we plan to add more seasons and cities and to test with grade 6–7 classes and screen-reader users.

Tools

  • Python (ffmpeg, Pillow, NumPy) to prepare frames.
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Canvas and the Web Audio API for the app.
  • Playwright for automated tests, flag-icons (MIT), and GitHub.
  • Hardware: ordinary laptops, tablets and phones.
  • Data: NASA SVS 5533 / GEOS-CF

How it is creative

Each pollutant is a "character" with its own voice, so students can tell four gases apart by ear. Sound and image play together, turning a scientific animation into a summer song for each city. Games turn listening into a challenge, and a mascot explains the data in kid-friendly words.
Factors we considered

  • Honesty with data: levels compare places on the map and are not health limits. Illustrative numbers, such as the Green Solutions cards, are labelled.
  • Musicality vs accuracy: a pentatonic scale keeps the sound pleasant, and we chose instruments by listening so that pitch changes are easy to hear.
  • Age and language: short sentences, Vietnamese and English, and simple layouts for grades 6–7.
  • Accessibility: sound-first design, read-aloud, labels for screen readers, and flag icons that also show on Windows.
  • Performance: all 300 frames are compressed into one file of about 15 MB.
